claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disease characterized by movement disorders, behavioral abnormalities, and brain atrophy.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an inherited neurodegenerative disease characterized by movement disorders, behavioral abnormalities, and brain atrophy (Orr and Zoghbi, 2007; Ross et al., 2014; Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Orr and Zoghbi, 2007; Ross et al., 2014; Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998).

claim: HD arises from mutations in Huntingtin (Htt) that expand a polyglutamine (polyQ)-encoding CAG repeat in exon 1 above a threshold length of 35 Qs.
source: HD arises from mutations in Huntingtin (Htt) that expand a polyglutamine (polyQ)-encoding CAG repeat in exon 1 above a threshold length of 35 Qs (MacDonald, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to MacDonald, 1993.

claim: The length of the polyQ tract correlates with both disease severity and propensity to form amyloid aggregates.
source: The length of the polyQ tract correlates with both disease severity and propensity to form amyloid aggregates (Scherzinger et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Scherzinger et al., 1999.

claim: Post-mortem analyses of HD brains contain amyloid aggregates formed primarily by N-terminal exon 1 truncations of Htt.
source: A link between neuronal toxicity and amyloid aggregation is further supported by post-mortem analyses of HD brains, which contain amyloid aggregates formed primarily by N-terminal exon 1 truncations of Htt (Difiglia, 1997; Landles et al., 2010; Mangiarini et al., 1996; Ross and Poirier, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published works (Difiglia, 1997; Landles et al., 2010; Mangiarini et al., 1996; Ross and Poirier, 2004).

claim: N-terminal Htt fragments may arise from aberrant splicing at the Htt exon 1 junction or from caspase cleavage.
source: Such N-terminal fragments may arise from aberrant splicing at the Htt exon 1 junction or from caspase cleavage (Sathasivam et al., 2013; Wellington et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Sathasivam et al., 2013; Wellington et al., 2002).

claim: Mutant Htt exon 1 carrying a polyQ expansion suffices to cause HD-like disease in animal models.
source: Importantly, mutant Htt exon 1 carrying a polyQ expansion (herein 'mHtt-Ex1') suffices to cause HD-like disease in animal models (Goldberg et al., 1996; Sathasivam et al., 2013; Wellington et al., 2002) and is thus widely used as a relevant model for HD biology and pathology.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Goldberg et al., 1996; Sathasivam et al., 2013; Wellington et al., 2002).

claim: One model proposes that amyloid aggregates are toxic because they sequester and deplete essential cellular proteins such as transcription factors or molecular chaperones.
source: One model proposes that amyloid aggregates are toxic because they sequester and deplete essential cellular proteins such as transcription factors or molecular chaperones (Kirstein-Miles et al., 2013; Olzscha et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Kirstein-Miles et al., 2013; Olzscha et al., 2011).

claim: The medium spiny striatal neurons more vulnerable to HD toxicity show few to no aggregates in HD patient brains.
source: For instance, the medium spiny striatal neurons more vulnerable to HD toxicity show few to no aggregates in HD patient brains. In contrast, less affected neuronal cell-types contain many aggregates (Kuemmerle et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kuemmerle et al., 1999.

claim: A longer N-terminal mHtt fragment encompassing exons 1 and 2 forms many aggregates in transgenic mice but exhibits no neuronal dysfunction.
source: In addition, while transgenic mHtt-Ex1 is neurotoxic in mice, a longer N-terminal mHtt fragment encompassing exons 1 and 2 forms many aggregates in transgenic mice but exhibits no neuronal dysfunction (Slow et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Slow et al., 2005.

claim: Longitudinal survival studies of primary neurons expressing fluorescently-tagged mHtt-Ex1 demonstrated that the formation of an amyloid inclusion correlated with neuronal survival.
source: Finally, longitudinal survival studies of primary neurons expressing fluorescently-tagged mHtt-Ex1 demonstrated that the formation of an amyloid inclusion correlated with neuronal survival (Arrasate et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Arrasate et al., 2004.

claim: mHtt can be sequestered in different types of cellular inclusions.
source: Since fluorescence and EM imaging studies have suggested that mHtt can be sequestered in different types of cellular inclusions (Caron et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2013; Nekooki-Machida et al., 2009; Sahl et al., 2016) one possible explanation for these observations is that only some inclusions are toxic, while others are protective.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published works (Caron et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2013; Nekooki-Machida et al., 2009; Sahl et al., 2016).

claim: An alternative hypothesis proposes that toxicity resides in soluble oligomeric mHtt conformations.
source: An alternative hypothesis proposes that toxicity resides in soluble oligomeric mHtt conformations (Behrends et al., 2006; Campioni et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five published works (Behrends et al., 2006; Campioni et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2015).

claim: Amyloidogenic proteins, including mHtt, populate an array of ill-defined soluble, oligomeric conformations.
source: Biophysical studies indicate that amyloidogenic proteins, including mHtt, not only form amyloid fibrils but also populate an array of ill-defined soluble, oligomeric conformations.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to biophysical studies, which is a form of citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Studies with conformationally-sensitive antibodies indicate that soluble oligomeric species are conformationally highly heterogeneous.
source: Studies with conformationally-sensitive antibodies indicate that these states are conformationally highly heterogeneous (Duim et al., 2014; Kayed and Glabe, 2006; Nucifora et al., 2012; Sontag et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four published works (Duim et al., 2014; Kayed and Glabe, 2006; Nucifora et al., 2012; Sontag et al., 2012).

claim: mHtt interactions with chaperones and degradation pathways are likely key determinants of the cellular balance of toxic and non-toxic conformers.
source: mHtt interactions with the chaperones and degradation pathways that handle misfolded proteins in the cell (Balch et al., 2008; Hartl et al., 2011) are likely key determinants of the cellular balance of toxic and non-toxic conformers.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Balch et al., 2008; Hartl et al., 2011) and represents an inference from the cited literature.

claim: N17, the 17 amino acid N-terminal flanking domain, has been shown to enhance mHtt aggregation.
source: N17, the 17 amino acid N-terminal flanking domain, has been shown to enhance mHtt aggregation (Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).

claim: N17 mediates mHtt interaction with chaperones.
source: N17 also mediates mHtt interaction with chaperones, hosts many post-translational modifications regulating mHtt toxicity (Gu et al., 2009; Steffan, 2004; Thompson et al., 2009), and harbors a functional nuclear export sequence (Maiuri et al., 2013; Rockabrand et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gu et al., 2009; Steffan, 2004; Thompson et al., 2009).

claim: N17 hosts many post-translational modifications regulating mHtt toxicity.
source: N17 also mediates mHtt interaction with chaperones, hosts many post-translational modifications regulating mHtt toxicity (Gu et al., 2009; Steffan, 2004; Thompson et al., 2009), and harbors a functional nuclear export sequence (Maiuri et al., 2013; Rockabrand et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gu et al., 2009; Steffan, 2004; Thompson et al., 2009).

claim: N17 harbors a functional nuclear export sequence.
source: N17 also mediates mHtt interaction with chaperones, hosts many post-translational modifications regulating mHtt toxicity (Gu et al., 2009; Steffan, 2004; Thompson et al., 2009), and harbors a functional nuclear export sequence (Maiuri et al., 2013; Rockabrand et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Maiuri et al., 2013; Rockabrand et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).

claim: The C-terminal proline-rich flanking domain (PRD) binds cellular factors and influences mHtt toxicity in yeast.
source: The C-terminal proline-rich flanking domain (herein 'PRD') also binds cellular factors and influences mHtt toxicity in yeast (Duennwald et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Duennwald et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2014).

claim: The PRD has been shown to slow aggregation.
source: The PRD has also been shown to slow aggregation (Bhattacharyya et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Bhattacharyya et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2009).

claim: Deletion of N17 reduces the rate and yield of amyloid formation and aggregation.
source: Consistent with previous reports, deletion of N17 reduces the rate and yield of amyloid formation and aggregation, while deletion of the PRD domain enhances formation of amyloids and aggregates (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) (Crick et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C, as well as citations to three published works (Crick et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).

claim: Deletion of the PRD domain enhances formation of amyloids and aggregates.
source: Consistent with previous reports, deletion of N17 reduces the rate and yield of amyloid formation and aggregation, while deletion of the PRD domain enhances formation of amyloids and aggregates (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) (Crick et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C, as well as citations to three published works (Crick et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009; Thakur et al., 2009).

claim: The elongation rate for amyloid formation and half-time to saturation of amyloid formation for mHtt variants lacking N17 (∆N and ∆N∆P) were much slower than those for mHtt variants containing N17 (Ex1 and ∆P).
source: Indeed, fitting the normalized ThioflavinT amyloid formation kinetics to the Finke-Watzky kinetic model (Alvarez et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2009) showed that the elongation rate v for amyloid formation and half-time to saturation of amyloid formation t1/2 for mHtt variants lacking N17 (∆N and ∆N∆P) were much slower than those for mHtt variants containing N17 (Ex1 and ∆P) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, and by citations to two published works (Alvarez et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2009) describing the kinetic model used.

claim: The presence of a PRD disfavors formation of large, SDS-insoluble aggregates while N17 exerts a dominant effect to promote the ThioflavinT-reactive, amyloid conformation.
source: We conclude that the presence of a PRD disfavors formation of large, SDS-insoluble aggregates while N17 exerts a dominant effect to promote the ThioflavinT-reactive, amyloid conformation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Deleting N17 reduced the formation of visible inclusions in vivo.
source: As observed in vitro, deleting N17 reduced the formation of visible inclusions in vivo, while deleting PRD enhanced the formation of aggregates (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Deleting PRD enhanced the formation of aggregates in vivo.
source: As observed in vitro, deleting N17 reduced the formation of visible inclusions in vivo, while deleting PRD enhanced the formation of aggregates (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Few aggregates were visible in the ∆N∆P expressing cells, despite rapid formation of insoluble aggregates in vitro.
source: Notably, few aggregates were visible in the ∆N∆P expressing cells, despite rapid formation of insoluble aggregates in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E-F (in vivo) and Figure 1B (in vitro).

claim: In the absence of the N17 and PRD flanking regions, the polyQ tract does not efficiently generate amyloidogenic fibrils but instead forms non-amyloidogenic aggregates that are less stable in vivo.
source: Given the slow kinetics of amyloid aggregation by ∆N∆P in vitro, it is possible that in the absence of the N17 and PRD flanking regions, the polyQ tract does not efficiently generate amyloidogenic fibrils but instead forms non-amyloidogenic aggregates that are less stable in vivo (Crick et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data and is supported by a citation to Crick et al., 2013.

claim: N17 and PRD have opposing effects on amyloid formation and aggregation in vitro and in vivo.
source: We conclude that N17 and PRD have opposing effects of on amyloid formation and aggregation in vitro and in vivo (Figure 1G) and further suggest that the cellular environment destabilizes the non-amyloid aggregates generated by the polyQ tract in ∆N∆P.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and is summarized in Figure 1G.

claim: The cellular environment destabilizes the non-amyloid aggregates generated by the polyQ tract in ∆N∆P.
source: We conclude that N17 and PRD have opposing effects of on amyloid formation and aggregation in vitro and in vivo (Figure 1G) and further suggest that the cellular environment destabilizes the non-amyloid aggregates generated by the polyQ tract in ∆N∆P.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: mHtt-Ex1 fibrils have a characteristic architecture, in which frayed fibril ends branch out from a bundled central core.
source: mHtt-Ex1 fibrils have a characteristic architecture, in which frayed fibril ends branch out from a bundled central core (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Bugg et al., 2012; Darrow et al., 2015; Shahmoradian et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, as well as citations to three published works (Bugg et al., 2012; Darrow et al., 2015; Shahmoradian et al., 2013).

claim: For the ∆N mHtt variant, dramatically fewer fibrils were observed, consistent with its lower amyloid aggregation propensity.
source: For the ∆N mHtt variant, we observed dramatically fewer fibrils, consistent with its lower amyloid aggregation propensity (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM observations and is consistent with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The fibrils formed by ∆N had a strikingly distinct morphology, which lacked the bundled architecture of Ex1 fibrils and were much thinner and straighter.
source: In addition, the fibrils formed by ∆N had a strikingly distinct morphology, which lacked the bundled architecture of Ex1 fibrils and were much thinner and straighter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Allowing ∆N aggregation to reach saturation by prolonged incubation increased the number of fibrils but did not change their thin morphology.
source: Allowing ∆N aggregation to reach saturation by prolonged incubation increased the number of fibrils but did not change their thin morphology (Figure 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The thin fibril structure of ∆N aggregates is intrinsic to the mutation.
source: Thus, the thin fibril structure of ∆N aggregates is intrinsic to the mutation.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that prolonged incubation did not change the thin morphology of ∆N fibrils.

claim: ∆P formed many large, densely packed aggregates with individual fibrils arranged in parallel bundles.
source: In contrast, ∆P formed many large, densely packed aggregates with individual fibrils arranged in parallel bundles (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), consistent with its increased aggregation propensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The morphology of ∆N∆P aggregates combined properties from both the ∆N and ∆P fibrils.
source: As observed for kinetic measurements, the morphology of ∆N∆P aggregates combined properties from both the ∆N and ∆P fibrils.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations.

claim: Similar to ∆N fibrils, the ∆N∆P fibrils were shorter, thinner and lacked the frayed fibril ends observed for Ex1.
source: Similar to ∆N fibrils, the ∆N∆P fibrils were shorter, thinner and lacked the frayed fibril ends observed for Ex1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2); similar to ∆P fibrils, ∆N∆P aggregates consisted of more densely packed fibrils (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar to ∆P fibrils, ∆N∆P aggregates consisted of more densely packed fibrils.
source: Similar to ∆N fibrils, the ∆N∆P fibrils were shorter, thinner and lacked the frayed fibril ends observed for Ex1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2); similar to ∆P fibrils, ∆N∆P aggregates consisted of more densely packed fibrils (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ∆N fibrils were only several nanometers in width, whereas Ex1 and ∆P fibrils were on average almost a micron wide and over a micron long.
source: Quantification of at least 10 individual micrographs for each fibril variant supported these observations, indicating that ∆N fibrils were only several nanometers in width, whereas Ex1 and ∆P fibrils were on average almost a micron wide and over a micron long (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: N17 and PRD have independent and dramatic effects on the amyloid formation propensity of the polyQ tract and its fibrillar structure.
source: We conclude that N17 and PRD have independent and dramatic effects on the amyloid formation propensity of the polyQ tract and its fibrillar structure.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and kinetic data.

claim: N17 promotes amyloid formation but also enhances interfibrillar contacts, thereby driving the bundling of individual fibrils observed for Ex1 and ∆P.
source: N17 promotes amyloid formation but also enhances interfibrillar contacts, thereby driving the bundling of individual fibrils observed for Ex1 and ∆P (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and is summarized in Figure 2B.

claim: PRD appears to destabilize lateral contacts among fibrils and thus prevents their dense packing.
source: In contrast, PRD appears to destabilize lateral contacts among fibrils and thus prevents their dense packing (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and is summarized in Figure 2B.

claim: The combined effects of N17 and PRD in Ex1 lead to the characteristic mHtt structure consisting of fibril bundles with frayed ends.
source: The combined effects of N17 and PRD in Ex1 lead to the characteristic mHtt structure consisting of fibril bundles with frayed ends (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and is summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: When N17 is absent, PRD leads to thin sparse fibrils observed for ∆N.
source: When N17 is absent, PRD leads to thin sparse fibrils observed for ∆N; while when PRD is absent, N17 leads to thick, bundled aggregates as observed for ∆P (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and is summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: When PRD is absent, N17 leads to thick, bundled aggregates as observed for ∆P.
source: When N17 is absent, PRD leads to thin sparse fibrils observed for ∆N; while when PRD is absent, N17 leads to thick, bundled aggregates as observed for ∆P (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations and is summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: For prions, distinct fibrillar amyloid stability is a hallmark of different prion strains.
source: For prions, distinct fibrillar amyloid stability is a hallmark of different prion strains (Tanaka et al., 2006) as their reduced stability (or increased 'frangibility') is directly linked to their propensity for intercellular transmission (Cushman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Tanaka et al., 2006; Cushman et al., 2010).

claim: Reduced stability (or increased 'frangibility') of prion fibrils is directly linked to their propensity for intercellular transmission.
source: For prions, distinct fibrillar amyloid stability is a hallmark of different prion strains (Tanaka et al., 2006) as their reduced stability (or increased 'frangibility') is directly linked to their propensity for intercellular transmission (Cushman et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cushman et al., 2010.

claim: mHtt fibrils formed by variants containing a PRD, namely Ex1 and ∆N, were readily fragmented into small, relatively homogeneous seeds of 30–50 nm in size.
source: DLS analyses confirmed that PRD significantly reduced the mechanical stability of mHtt aggregates. mHtt fibrils formed by variants containing a PRD, namely Ex1 and ∆N, were readily fragmented into small, relatively homogeneous seeds of 30–50 nm in size (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DLS data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Aggregates formed by mHtt variants lacking a PRD, namely ∆P and ∆N∆P, resisted disruption and remained in large and highly bundled fibrillar structures ranging from 0.3–2 µm even at the harshest sonication conditions.
source: In contrast, aggregates formed by mHtt variants lacking a PRD, namely ∆P and ∆N∆P, resisted disruption and remained in large and highly bundled fibrillar structures ranging from 0.3–2 µm even at the harshest sonication conditions (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by DLS and cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3B-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sonicated seeds of Ex1 and ∆N were small structures only one or two fibrils in width, while the sonication products of ∆P and ∆N∆P were large, thick, and densely-packed bundles of fibers.
source: Cryo-EM imaging confirmed and extended these observations (Figure 3C). The sonicated seeds of Ex1 and ∆N were small structures only one or two fibrils in width, while the sonication products of ∆P and ∆N∆P were large, thick, and densely-packed bundles of fibers.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence or absence of N17 had no significant impact on the size of the fragmented species.
source: Of note, the presence or absence of N17 had no significant impact on the size of the fragmented species, indicating that while N17 contributes to the formation of these fibrils, it does not contribute to their mechanical stability.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the DLS and cryo-EM data.

claim: While N17 contributes to the formation of fibrils, it does not contribute to their mechanical stability.
source: Of note, the presence or absence of N17 had no significant impact on the size of the fragmented species, indicating that while N17 contributes to the formation of these fibrils, it does not contribute to their mechanical stability.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the DLS and cryo-EM data.

claim: The PRD mechanically destabilizes mHtt aggregates by disfavoring inter-fibrillar contacts.
source: We conclude that the PRD mechanically destabilizes mHtt aggregates by disfavoring inter-fibrillar contacts (Figure 2A), thus providing a molecular basis for reduced aggregation propensity of mHtt variants with a PRD (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the sonication and cryo-EM data shown in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: Both Ex1 and ∆P fibrils were similarly resistant to intermediate concentrations of formic acid.
source: Both Ex1 and ∆P fibrils were similarly resistant to intermediate concentrations of formic acid and only following incubation with 100% formic acid, which can dissolve mHtt aggregates formed in vivo (Hazeki et al., 2000), did we observe significant denaturation of the mHtt fibrils of both Ex1 and ∆P (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: 100% formic acid can dissolve mHtt aggregates formed in vivo.
source: Both Ex1 and ∆P fibrils were similarly resistant to intermediate concentrations of formic acid and only following incubation with 100% formic acid, which can dissolve mHtt aggregates formed in vivo (Hazeki et al., 2000), did we observe significant denaturation of the mHtt fibrils of both Ex1 and ∆P (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hazeki et al., 2000.

claim: The mechanical stability differences for fibrils with or without the PRD derives from their structural architecture rather than intrinsic differences in their chemical stability.
source: These experiments suggest that the mechanical stability differences for fibrils with or without the PRD derives from their structural architecture rather than intrinsic differences in their chemical stability.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the formic acid denaturation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Native oligomers of Ex1 appeared early during aggregation kinetics and gradually decreased as aggregation proceeded to form the aggregates retained in the filter trap.
source: Native-AGE gel analyses revealed that native oligomers of Ex1 appeared early during aggregation kinetics and gradually decreased as aggregation proceeded to form the aggregates retained in the filter trap (Figure 4B–C) (Sontag et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C and a citation to Sontag et al., 2012.

claim: Large SDS-soluble oligomers appeared to increase over time in the SDS-AGE gel.
source: In contrast, large SDS-soluble oligomers appeared to increase over time in the SDS-AGE gel (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ∆P had much fewer oligomers in both native- and SDS-AGE gels.
source: By contrast, ∆P had much fewer oligomers in both native- and SDS-AGE gels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The native oligomers of ∆P disappeared much more rapidly during the time-course of aggregation than those observed for Ex1.
source: Furthermore, the native oligomers disappeared much more rapidly during the time-course of aggregation that those observed for Ex1, consistent with the overall faster aggregation of ∆P.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The absence of PRD alters the balance between oligomer and fibril formation, perhaps by allowing faster progression of these oligomeric species to aggregates.
source: Thus, the absence of PRD alters the balance between oligomer and fibril formation, perhaps by allowing faster progression of these oligomeric species to aggregates (Figure 1B-C, 4D).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 4D.

claim: Very large ∆N oligomers persisted through the aggregation reaction in both the native-AGE and SDS-AGE gels.
source: Surprisingly, very large ∆N oligomers persisted through the aggregation reaction in both the native-AGE and SDS-AGE gels (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Even after 60 hr, when ∆N amyloid aggregation was saturated, the population of ∆N oligomers remained under both native and mildly denaturing conditions.
source: Even after 60 hr, when ∆N amyloid aggregation was saturated, the population of ∆N oligomers remained under both native and mildly denaturing conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The increased presence of ∆N oligomers resulted in few filter-trap retained aggregates.
source: Consistent with our previous data, the increased presence of ∆N oligomers resulted in few filter-trap retained aggregates (Figure 1B–C, 4C).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 4C.

claim: Large ∆N oligomers were already abundant as early as 3 hr post-aggregation.
source: However, while large ∆N oligomers were already abundant as early as 3 hr post-aggregation (Figure 4B–C), cryo-EM imaging of ∆N at 3 hr of aggregation showed very few fibrils and no additional identifiable densities or structures (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Cryo-EM imaging of ∆N at 3 hr of aggregation showed very few fibrils and no additional identifiable densities or structures.
source: However, while large ∆N oligomers were already abundant as early as 3 hr post-aggregation (Figure 4B–C), cryo-EM imaging of ∆N at 3 hr of aggregation showed very few fibrils and no additional identifiable densities or structures (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM observations.

claim: The amyloidogenic, ThioflavinT-reactive species formed by ∆N only accumulated significantly after 30 hr of aggregation.
source: Furthermore the amyloidogenic, ThioflavinT-reactive species formed by ∆N only accumulated significantly after 30 hr of aggregation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ∆N becomes trapped forming stable soluble oligomers that may be mildly SDS-resistant but are neither fibrillar nor amyloid.
source: Together, these data indicate that ∆N becomes trapped forming stable soluble oligomers that may be mildly SDS-resistant but are neither fibrillar nor amyloid.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the AGE, cryo-EM, and ThioflavinT data.

claim: ∆N oligomers, despite being very large in size, appear to be too structurally heterogeneous to yield identifiable diffraction signatures by cryoEM.
source: These ∆N oligomers, despite being very large in size, appear to be too structurally heterogeneous to yield identifiable diffraction signatures by cryoEM.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cryo-EM observations.

claim: All mHtt variants formed several small oligomer species very early in the aggregation reaction.
source: Interestingly, all mHtt variants formed several small oligomer species very early in the aggregation reaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 4Di.

claim: For Ex1 and ∆P, small oligomers disappeared as aggregation progressed, while the species of ∆N and ∆N∆P were very stable.
source: For Ex1 and ∆P, these small oligomers disappeared as aggregation progressed, while the species of ∆N and ∆N∆P were very stable, similar to that observed for large oligomers in SDS-AGE gels (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 4Di and SDS-AGE data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: N17 promotes the formation of fibrils at the expense of oligomer formation, whereas the PRD contributes to the accumulation of oligomers.
source: This analysis supports the view that N17 promotes the formation of fibrils (Figure 2) at the expense of oligomer formation, whereas the PRD contributes to the accumulation of oligomers.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the AGE and Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: N17 and PRD seem to act independently in oligomer formation since the oligomers formed by ∆N∆P exhibited a behavior intermediate between the ∆N and ∆P phenotypes in the AGE oligomer assays.
source: Interestingly, N17 and PRD seem to act independently in oligomer formation since the oligomers formed by ∆N∆P exhibited a behavior intermediate between the ∆N and ∆P phenotypes in the AGE oligomer assays.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the AGE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant amount of ∆N∆P species progressed to the insoluble aggregates.

Indeed, their distinct migration patterns in Native-AGE and Blue-Native PAGE, which separate oligomers based on a number of shape, size and exposed charge characteristics, seems to support this hypothesis.

claim: The rate of oligomer disappearance was enhanced at higher N17 concentrations.

evidence: The claim is supported by SDS-AGE data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: N17 triggers a conformational switch that disfavors the accumulation of trapped, oligomeric species and allows the formation of amyloid fibrils.

claim: N17 promoted disappearance of pre-formed, non-amyloidogenic oligomers.

claim: N17 can act on the kinetically trapped ∆N oligomers themselves to promote formation of amyloid fibrils.
source: Strikingly, N17 also promoted disappearance of these pre-formed, non-amyloidogenic oligomers (Figure 5D), suggesting that N17 can act on the kinetically trapped ∆N oligomers themselves to promote formation of amyloid fibrils (Figure 5B).

claim: N17 did not promote inclusion formation in ST14a cells expressing the non-pathogenic Q-length Htt-Ex1-Q25-YFP.

claim: N17 trans addition can increase mHtt aggregation in vivo.
source: These results indicate that, N17 trans addition can increase mHtt aggregation in vivo.

claim: ∆N forms many oligomers and few fibrillar aggregates.

claim: ∆P forms many fibrillar aggregates and few oligomers.
source: Specifically, ∆N forms many oligomers and few fibrillar aggregates; ∆P forms many fibrillar aggregates and few oligomers; and ∆N∆P, which is essentially a pathogenic length Q-tract, forms both oligomers and fibrils (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1-4 and summarized in Figure 6A.

claim: ∆N∆P, which is essentially a pathogenic length Q-tract, forms both oligomers and fibrils.
source: Specifically, ∆N forms many oligomers and few fibrillar aggregates; ∆P forms many fibrillar aggregates and few oligomers; and ∆N∆P, which is essentially a pathogenic length Q-tract, forms both oligomers and fibrils (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1-4 and summarized in Figure 6A.

claim: Corticostriatal brain slices provide a more disease relevant, 'tissue contextual' model of HD when compared to traditional models of neuronal cell cultures.
source: To evaluate the toxicity of these polyQ expanded mHtt variants we looked at the striatal neurons of rat corticostriatal brain slices, which provide a more disease relevant, 'tissue contextual' model of HD when compared to traditional models of neuronal cell cultures (Khoshnan et al., 2004; Reinhart et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Khoshnan et al., 2004; Reinhart et al., 2011).

claim: In corticostriatal brain slices, the striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), which are preferentially affected in HD, remain within their intact local tissue environment and maintain interactions among multiple brain cell-types.
source: In corticostriatal brain slices, the striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), which are preferentially affected in HD, remain within their intact local tissue environment and maintain interactions among multiple brain cell-types.
evidence: The claim is a statement of established knowledge about the corticostriatal brain slice model.

claim: When corticostriatal brain slices are transfected with polyQ-expanded mHtt there is a progressive degeneration of MSNs over 3–5 days.
source: Importantly, when corticostriatal brain slices are transfected with polyQ-expanded mHtt there is a progressive degeneration of MSNs over 3–5 days (Reinhart et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinhart et al., 2011.

claim: No degeneration is observed when YFP is co-transfected with Htt carrying non-pathogenic polyQ repeats (Q8, Q23) or with a control vector.
source: No degeneration is observed when YFP is co-transfected with Htt carrying non-pathogenic polyQ repeats (Q8, Q23) or with a control vector (Reinhart et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reinhart et al., 2011.

claim: ∆N and ∆P were as toxic as Ex1 as early as 3 days after transfection.
source: Surprisingly, when the mHtt-Ex1 variants were transfected into brain slices, there were striking discrepancies between their toxicity and their structural properties. Although ∆N and ∆P have dramatically different aggregation and oligomerization propensities in vitro and in vivo, both were as toxic as Ex1 as early as 3 days after transfection (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: ∆N∆P exhibited only modest toxicity even by day 4.
source: Even more surprisingly, ∆N∆P, which generates both aggregates and oligomers and has an expanded polyQ tract of identical length, exhibited only modest toxicity even by day 4 (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Since both ∆N, which forms few amyloid fibrils, and ∆P, which forms few oligomers are both highly toxic, the data cannot be explained by either fibrillar aggregates or oligomeric species per se as being toxic.
source: Since both ∆N, which forms few amyloid fibrils, and ∆P, which forms few oligomers are both highly toxic, our data cannot be explained by either fibrillar aggregates or, oligomeric species per se as being toxic.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity data shown in Figure 6 and the structural data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: Since the expanded polyQ tract itself is only mildly toxic, the action of the flanking regions must be key to induce the toxic polyQ conformation(s).
source: Remarkably, since the expanded polyQ tract itself is only mildly toxic, the action of the flanking regions must be key to induce the toxic polyQ conformation(s).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity data shown in Figure 6.

claim: mHtt toxicity in the brain slices was observed for those variants that gave rise to 3B5H10-reactive small oligomers, namely Ex1, ∆N and ∆P but not ∆N∆P.
source: However, it was intriguing that mHtt toxicity in the brain slices was observed for those variants that gave rise to 3B5H10-reactive small oligomers, namely Ex1, ∆N and ∆P but not ∆N∆P.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity data shown in Figure 6 and the 3B5H10 reactivity data shown in Figure 4Dii.

claim: Striatal-derived neurons expressing the toxic variants Ex1, ∆N and ∆P contained a diffusely localized 3B5H10-reactive species that was absent in cells expressing the less toxic ∆N∆P.
source: Indeed, immunofluorescence analysis showed that striatal-derived neurons expressing the toxic variants Ex1, ∆N and ∆P contained a diffusely localized 3B5H10-reactive species that was absent in cells expressing the less toxic ∆N∆P (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Little 3B5H10 reactivity was observed in neurons expressing Htt-Ex1 construct with a non-pathogenic polyQ length.
source: Little 3B5H10 reactivity was observed in neurons expressing Htt-Ex1 construct with a non-pathogenic polyQ length (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), similar to a previous report (Miller et al., 2011).

claim: 3B5H10 did not stain large mHtt aggregates or inclusions.
source: Of note, 3B5H10 did not stain large mHtt aggregates or inclusions (Figure 7C), suggesting that in vivo the 3B5H10-reactive conformation is excluded from large aggregates.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In vivo the 3B5H10-reactive conformation is excluded from large aggregates.
source: Of note, 3B5H10 did not stain large mHtt aggregates or inclusions (Figure 7C), suggesting that in vivo the 3B5H10-reactive conformation is excluded from large aggregates.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: GFP immunoblotting of the Blue-Native PAGE revealed variant-specific single bands, suggesting that each variant forms a predominant small oligomeric species in vivo.
source: GFP immunoblotting of the Blue-Native PAGE revealed variant-specific single bands, suggesting that, unlike what we observed in vitro each variant forms a predominant small oligomeric species in vivo (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The larger mHtt oligomers observed in vivo displayed a heterogeneous spectrum of sizes as observed with purified mHtt.
source: In contrast, the larger mHtt oligomers observed in vivo displayed a heterogeneous spectrum of sizes as observed with purified mHtt.

claim: The only 3B5H10-reactive species formed in vivo were the small mHtt oligomers detected in the Blue-Native PAGE.

evidence: The claim is supported by Blue-Native PAGE data shown in Figure 7D.

source: The polyQ tract itself can clearly generate different oligomer populations, but formation of oligomer conformations reactive to 3B5H10 requires either the N17 or PRD domain.

claim: The similar 3B5H10 reactivity of Ex1, ∆N, ∆P and ∆N∆P in vitro and in vivo suggests that the conformational differences among these mHtt variants is intrinsic to the structural influence of the flanking regions on the polyQ region.
source: The similar 3B5H10 reactivity of Ex1, ∆N, ∆P and ∆N∆P in vitro and in vivo suggests that the conformational differences among these mHtt variants is intrinsic to the structural influence of the flanking regions on the polyQ region.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the 3B5H10 reactivity data shown in Figures 4Dii and 7D.

claim: The chaperonin TRiC/CCT suppresses mHtt aggregation and toxicity in many HD models through recognition of N17 by the CCT1 subunit.
source: One established mechanism is the chaperonin TRiC/CCT, which suppresses mHtt aggregation and toxicity in many HD models through recognition of N17 by the CCT1 subunit (Behrends et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2006; Tam et al., 2009).

claim: Overexpression of CCT1 or exogenous addition of the purified substrate-binding domain of CCT1 (ApiCCT1) to the media suffices to suppress mHtt toxicity in neuronal cell culture.
source: In neuronal cell culture, overexpression of CCT1 or exogenous addition of the purified substrate-binding domain of CCT1 (ApiCCT1) to the media suffices to suppress mHtt toxicity (Kitamura et al., 2006; Sontag et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Kitamura et al., 2006; Sontag et al., 2013; Tam et al., 2009).

source: Indeed, exogenous administration of purified recombinant ApiCCT1 significantly protected MSNs from mHtt neurotoxicity in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 7Ei).

claim: Chaperonin protection against HD toxicity decreases the levels of 3B5H10-reactive soluble species.
source: These experiments support the notion that these 3B5H10-reactive small oligomers are diagnostic of a conformational pathway linked to toxicity and that chaperonin protection against HD toxicity decreases the levels of these soluble species.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the ApiCCT1 experiments shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Overexpression of CCT1 dramatically protected MSNs from mHtt-Ex1 toxicity but did not protect MSNs from ∆N-induced toxicity.

claim: N17 hosts the CCT1 binding site in mHtt.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that N17 hosts the CCT1 binding site in mHtt (Tam et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tam et al., 2009.

claim: Despite the presence of N17, CCT1 afforded only a modest degree of protection for ∆P-induced toxicity.
source: Surprisingly, despite the presence of N17, CCT1 afforded only a modest degree of protection for ∆P-induced toxicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The minimal rescue of ∆P by CCT1 may be due to the aggressive neurotoxicity of ∆P, which may impair neurons too quickly to be effectively rescued by CCT1.
source: The minimal rescue of ∆P by CCT1 may be due to the aggressive neurotoxicity of ∆P (Figure 6C–E), which may impair neurons too quickly to be effectively rescued by CCT1.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the toxicity data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: The absence of the PRD domain may reduce the availability of N17 to engage CCT1.
source: Alternatively, we considered that the absence of the PRD domain may reduce the availability of N17 to engage CCT1.

claim: N17 contains a nuclear export sequence.
source: First, N17 contains a nuclear export sequence (Gu et al., 2015; Maiuri et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2013), leading ∆N variants to accumulate in the nucleus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Gu et al., 2015; Maiuri et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2013).

claim: ∆N variants accumulate in the nucleus.
source: First, N17 contains a nuclear export sequence (Gu et al., 2015; Maiuri et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2013), leading ∆N variants to accumulate in the nucleus. In striatal-derived neurons, we confirmed that mHtt-Ex1 was both cytoplasmic and nuclear while ∆N was enriched in the nucleus (Figure 8C).

claim: mHtt-Ex1 was both cytoplasmic and nuclear while ∆N was enriched in the nucleus.
source: In striatal-derived neurons, we confirmed that mHtt-Ex1 was both cytoplasmic and nuclear while ∆N was enriched in the nucleus (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: ∆P was enriched in the nucleus, even though it contains the N17 domain.
source: Surprisingly, ∆P was also enriched in the nucleus, even though it contains the N17 domain (Figure 8C), further suggesting that the PRD region may regulate the exposure of N17.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The PRD region may regulate the exposure of N17.
source: Surprisingly, ∆P was also enriched in the nucleus, even though it contains the N17 domain (Figure 8C), further suggesting that the PRD region may regulate the exposure of N17.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: N17 is proposed to promote mHtt degradation.
source: Second, N17 is also proposed to promote mHtt degradation (Thompson et al., 2009), which occurs via the ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways (Thompson et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Thompson et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2013).

claim: mHtt degradation occurs via the ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways.
source: Second, N17 is also proposed to promote mHtt degradation (Thompson et al., 2009), which occurs via the ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways (Thompson et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Thompson et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2013).

claim: Both ∆N and ∆P had significantly slower protein clearance rates compared to Ex1.
source: Notably, both ∆N and ∆P had significantly slower protein clearance rates compared to Ex1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pulse-chase data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Efficient mHtt recognition by the cellular degradation pathways requires the presence of both polyQ-flanking domains.

claim: N17 was significantly more protease-sensitive in Ex1 oligomers containing the PRD than in ∆P oligomers.

evidence: The claim is supported by Proteinase K digestion data shown in Figure 8Eii-iii.

claim: N17 in Ex1 oligomers was much more sensitive to trypsin protease cleavage than in ∆P oligomers.
source: Indeed, N17 in Ex1 oligomers was much more sensitive to trypsin protease cleavage than in ∆P oligomers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by trypsin digestion data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The PRD increases exposure of the N17 domain.
source: Thus, these experiments show that the PRD increases exposure of the N17 domain, which explains the similar responses of ∆N and ∆P to CCT1 protection, their enhanced nuclear localization and their slower protein degradation kinetics, all of which were previously shown to depend on N17 (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the protease digestion data shown in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Despite their opposing effects on the energetics of aggregation or oligomer formation, the two polyQ flanking regions also act synergistically in vivo to determine the cellular fate of mHtt.
source: Taken together, these analyses indicate that, despite their opposing effects on the energetics of aggregation or oligomer formation, the two polyQ flanking regions also act synergistically in vivo to determine the cellular fate of mHtt (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: mHtt structural conformers and their cellular interactions are more relevant to pathogenesis than polyQ aggregation propensity.
source: Overall, these results have two major implications. Firstly, mHtt structural conformers and their cellular interactions are more relevant to pathogenesis than polyQ aggregation propensity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity and structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only certain conformational sub-populations of mHtt are neurotoxic.
source: The Ex1, ∆N and ∆P variants are all highly toxic (Figure 6C–E) despite their different propensities to form insoluble aggregates or soluble oligomers both in vitro and in vivo (Figure 1B-C, 4B-E, 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). This suggests that only certain conformational sub-populations are neurotoxic (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity and structural data shown in Figures 1, 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Since polyQ alone generates toxic conformations inefficiently, the sequence context is key to the neurotoxic structural transition.
source: Secondly, since polyQ alone generates toxic conformations inefficiently, the sequence context is key to the neurotoxic structural transition.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the toxicity data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The other polyQ-expansion disease causing proteins, such as ataxins, must contain additional sequence elements that are functionally equivalent to N17 or the PRD.
source: Thus, the other polyQ-expansion disease causing proteins, such as ataxins (Almeida et al., 2013) must contain additional sequence elements that are functionally equivalent to N17 or the PRD.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings about N17 and PRD, and is supported by a citation to Almeida et al., 2013.

claim: Despite their distinct intrinsic effects in stabilizing either the oligomer or fibrillar states, N17 and PRD cooperate in vivo to determine mHtt fate.

claim: While N17 contains the recognition site for CCT1 and is known to promote mHtt degradation, both N17 and PRD are required for efficient CCT1-mediated neuroprotection and clearance of soluble mHtt species.
source: While N17 contains the recognition site for CCT1 and is known to promote mHtt degradation, both N17 and PRD are required for efficient CCT1-mediated neuroprotection (Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and clearance of soluble mHtt species (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 8B, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 8D.

claim: N17 is essential to prevent the accumulation of mHtt in the nucleus.
source: N17 is also essential to prevent the accumulation of mHtt in the nucleus (Gu et al., 2015), but deletion of PRD also causes nuclear-enrichment of mHtt toxic species, which may play an enhanced role in Htt pathogenesis (Difiglia, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of PRD causes nuclear-enrichment of mHtt toxic species, which may play an enhanced role in Htt pathogenesis.
source: N17 is also essential to prevent the accumulation of mHtt in the nucleus (Gu et al., 2015), but deletion of PRD also causes nuclear-enrichment of mHtt toxic species, which may play an enhanced role in Htt pathogenesis (Difiglia, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and a citation to Difiglia, 1997.

claim: The observed synergy of the flanking regions in vivo is rooted in the conformational modulation exerted by the PRD to promote exposure of N17.

evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The PRD may directly enhance N17 availability through transient interactions with each other.
source: One model for this is the PRD may directly enhance N17 availability through transient interactions with each other (Behrends et al., 2006; Caron et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by citations to two published works (Behrends et al., 2006; Caron et al., 2013).

claim: The structural hindrance imposed by the PRD may prevent N17 from becoming buried in the early stages of oligomerization.
source: Alternatively, the structural hindrance imposed by the PRD may prevent N17 from becoming buried in the early stages of oligomerization (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both proteostasis and nucleo-cytoplasmic trafficking decrease during aging.
source: Both proteostasis (Brehme et al., 2014; Taylor and Dillin, 2011) and nucleo-cytoplasmic trafficking (D'Angelo et al., 2009) decrease during aging.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published works (Brehme et al., 2014; Taylor and Dillin, 2011; D'Angelo et al., 2009).

claim: As a neuron's ability to clear mHtt declines, the ensuing accumulation of soluble species may exert further toxicity.
source: As a neuron's ability to clear mHtt declines, the ensuing accumulation of soluble species may exert further toxicity (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the model shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Toxic, off-pathway oligomers are also reported for α-synuclein, emphasizing the potential toxicity of soluble species that cannot be sequestered into larger aggregates.
source: With age or the absence of N17, toxic oligomeric species accumulate, thereby exerting cellular damage. Of note, toxic, off-pathway oligomers are also reported for α-synuclein, emphasizing the potential toxicity of soluble species that cannot be sequestered into larger aggregates (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: Effective therapeutics for HD should impact the conformers associated with toxicity.
source: Our study suggests that effective therapeutics for HD should impact the conformers associated with toxicity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: TRiC promotes clearance of small 3B5H10-reactive mHtt oligomers confirming its crucial protective role in HD.
source: We show that TRiC, previously shown to interact with mHtt monomers (Tam et al., 2009), large oligomers (Sontag et al., 2013) and fibrillar aggregates (Shahmoradian et al., 2013), promotes clearance of small 3B5H10-reactive mHtt oligomers (Figure 7E) confirming its crucial protective role in HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and citations to three published works (Tam et al., 2009; Sontag et al., 2013; Shahmoradian et al., 2013).

claim: mHtt clearance rate in neurons is linked to their likelihood of survival.
source: In addition, mHtt clearance rate in neurons is linked to their likelihood of survival (Tsvetkov et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsvetkov et al., 2013.

claim: Enhancing the ability of mHtt flanking regions to engage proteostasis pathways could provide highly specific and potent HD therapeutics.
source: Thus, enhancing the ability of mHtt flanking regions to engage proteostasis pathways could provide highly specific and potent HD therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Htt contains a methionine at residue 8 which could be used as an alternative translation initiation site, leading to a partial truncation of N17.
source: Htt contains a methionine at residue 8 which could be used as an alternative translation initiation site, leading to a partial truncation of N17.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the known sequence of Htt.

claim: Proline-repeat stretches can stall translation.
source: Likewise, it has long been observed that proline-repeat stretches can stall translation (Gutierrez et al., 2013; Ude et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published works (Gutierrez et al., 2013; Ude et al., 2013).

claim: Proline-dependent stalling may generate a partially truncated '∆P-like' mHtt-Ex1 variant.
source: For mHtt, this proline-dependent stalling may generate a partially truncated '∆P-like' mHtt-Ex1 variant.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the known property of proline-repeat stretches to stall translation.
